title: Why the Black Sea Is So Dangerous Right Now — And Why It Affects Your Bread
summary:
Imagine a sea where ships are afraid to sail. That's the Black Sea right now.

Since July, more than 210 strikes have hit commercial ships there. That's according to Ambrey, a British company that tracks risks at sea. It says Ukraine was behind 125 of the strikes and Russia behind 88.

Why does this matter to you? Russia and Ukraine grow about a quarter of the world's wheat. Wheat is used to make bread, pasta, and cereal. Because of the fighting, their combined exports are down 60% from last year. That means wheat prices are going up around the world.

Mykola Lupar is a 29-year-old commander in Ukraine's navy. He patrols from the port of Chornomorsk. He says his crew only has minutes on the water before they must rush back to shore. "It's very dangerous," he said.

Russia says it only targets military assets. Ukraine says Russia is hitting civilian ships. In July, a missile strike killed 10 people on a ship called the Golden Leo near Odesa. Ukraine said it was carrying corn.

Turkey has tried to make a truce so ships can sail safely. So far, it hasn't worked.
why_it_matters: When ships are too scared to sail, the wheat that becomes your bread, pasta and cereal costs more — even in a grocery store far away from the Black Sea.

keywords.explanation: Commercial ships are ships that carry goods to sell, not warships.
Exports are the goods a country sells and sends to other countries.
A truce is an agreement to stop fighting for a while.
A missile strike is an attack with a fast-flying weapon that explodes when it hits.
Military assets are army things like warships, bases and weapons — not ordinary ships carrying food.
A commander is the person in charge of a group of sailors or soldiers.

questions.question: Since July, how many strikes have hit commercial ships in the Black Sea?
Which company tracks risks at sea and counted the strikes?
About how much of the world's wheat do Russia and Ukraine grow?
Where does commander Mykola Lupar patrol from?
What did Ukraine say the ship Golden Leo was carrying when a missile strike killed 10 people?
Which country has tried to make a truce so ships can sail safely?

background_read: The Black Sea (a sea bordered by countries such as Ukraine, Russia and Turkey) is one of the world's main routes for shipping grain — the seeds used to make flour, bread and pasta.
Ukraine and Russia are often called the 'breadbasket of the world' because so much of the wheat people eat grows on their farms.
Turkey (a country that sits between Europe and Asia) controls the narrow straits that ships must pass through to leave the Black Sea and reach the open sea, which is why it is trying to make a truce.
Article_Structure: WHO: Ukraine and Russia are the two sides hitting ships in the Black Sea, Turkey is trying to make a truce, and Ukraine's navy — including commander Mykola Lupar — patrols from the port of Chornomorsk.
WHAT: More than 210 strikes have hit commercial ships since July (125 blamed on Ukraine, 88 on Russia), and the two countries' wheat exports are down 60% from last year.
WHERE: The Black Sea, especially near the Ukrainian port of Odesa, where a missile strike killed 10 people on a ship called the Golden Leo.
WHY: Russia and Ukraine grow about a quarter of the world's wheat, so the danger at sea is pushing up bread, pasta and cereal prices around the world.

perspectives.description: They say Russia is hitting civilian ships — like the Golden Leo, which Ukraine says was carrying corn — and their crews only have minutes on the water before rushing back to shore because it is so dangerous.
Russia says it only targets military assets, meaning it claims its strikes are aimed at army things, not ordinary ships carrying food.
Turkey wants a truce so ships can sail safely again, and risk trackers like Ambrey count every strike so sailors and shipping companies know how dangerous the water is.
